info.desc: 2112 ("Twenty-One Twelve") is the fourth studio album by Canadian progressive rock band Rush, released in 1976. The Toronto dates of the 2112 tour were recorded and released as All The World's a Stage in September 1976. In 2006 a poll of Planet Rock listeners picked 2112 as the definitive Rush album. The album 2112 features an eponymous seven-part suite written by Geddy Lee and Alex Lifeson, with lyrics written by Neil Peart. The suite tells a dystopian story set in the year 2112. Since the album is named after the suite it is mistakenly thought of as a concept .

podcast.body: This album is a complex concept record featuring a narrative that includes the Red Star, the Solar Federation, and priests controlling existence in the temples of Syrikes. The story also involves a rebel guitar player who rises up and commits suicide. The entire work was inspired by the objectiveist philosopher Ayn Rand, particularly her books like *Atlas Shrugged*. "We've got the Red Star, the Solar Federation, and the priests who run the temples of Syrikes in their command over existence. And then we have the rebel guitar player who rises up and then commits suicide."

podcast.body: This album was a "make or break" record for Rush, following the commercial disappointment of their third album, *Caress of Steel*. It proved to be a major success, described as "hitting it out of the park." The entire first side of the album is a concept piece, blending Prog Rock with sci-fi themes. It draws inspiration from Ayn Rand's 1937 novel *Anthem*, portraying a dystopian society where music and individualism are outlawed. The album's narrative is set in the future city of Megadon, where priests and computers suppress creativity, before the Solar Federation and an unnamed entity take control. The album is fundamentally a song cycle about the rediscovery of music. "This was a maker break record for Rush."
